passage: The auto-rickshaw driver was already honking when Joseph, Anjali's partner, said, "You forgot to book the cab again. That's why we're late." Anjali's face went hot. "I told you Tuesday that I was busy, and you never checked either, and honestly last month you..." The train departed in eighteen minutes, and the words kept coming, each one a small wall. Then Anjali caught Joseph's tired face at the auto's edge. A breath. "Wait. You're right. I forgot to book it, and I should have said so. I'm sorry." Joseph blinked. "Thank you," Joseph said. "I was stressed too." "Yes," Anjali said. "Let's get to the station. We'll talk about the checking thing tonight." They made the train with four minutes to spare.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the train departed at the start of the argument?
Why did Anjali start with explanations and counter-blame?
qa.a: Criticism seemed to feel like being unlovable, so Anjali reached for excuses and Joseph's own lapses, building a wall of words.

qa.q: What changed when Anjali breathed and spoke again, and what could Anjali keep doing?
qa.a: Anjali said what was true in the complaint and apologised before defending, which let Joseph soften. Anjali could keep answering the complaint first and raise the checking issue later.

qa.q: How does Joseph likely experience the two responses from Anjali?
qa.a: The first probably felt like being blamed back in a rush, while the second, "You're right," lets Joseph say "I was stressed too" and lowers the tension.

grounding: Shows a partner who explains, denies and counter-blames when a fault is named, then breathes, says what is true in it and answers the complaint first.

passage:
I'm Kiran, and here's what I used to do every time. Uday would say something like, "You were on your phone the whole dinner with my parents." And before he'd finished, I'd be talking. "I had a work message. You were on your phone last week. Why do you always attack me?" Explain, deny, blame. In about four seconds.

It felt like survival. Any criticism landed like: you are unlovable.

Last Sunday it happened again. He said I never ask about his day. I felt my mouth open, the defence ready.

I breathed instead. One long breath. Then I said, "That's true. I haven't been asking. I'm sorry." Just that.

Uday looked shocked, then his face softened. "Thank you. That's all I wanted."

Later I said, "I get defensive because criticism feels like you don't love me." He said, "It's the opposite. I say it because I want us close."

qa.q: What did Uday say Kiran never asks about?
qa.a: Uday said Kiran never asks about his day.

qa.q: Why did Kiran react so quickly with explanations and blame?
qa.a: Kiran felt that any criticism meant being unlovable, so defensiveness felt like survival, driven by fear and hurt.

qa.q: What did Kiran do differently last Sunday?
qa.a: Kiran took a breath, admitted what was true in the complaint, and apologised before explaining anything.

qa.q: How does Uday see his own criticism?
qa.a: Uday sees it as a way to stay close, not an attack, saying he raises things because he wants them close.

grounding: The reflection shows a young spouse who meets criticism with instant defence because it feels like being unlovable, and learns to breathe and own what is true.

passage:
Couples counsellor's note, session 4, Saurabh and Rashmi.

Today Rashmi said, calmly, that Saurabh leaves all the planning of family events to her. Before she had finished, Saurabh was answering: "That's not true, I booked the cab for Diwali, and you never let me plan anyway, and your mother..." He spoke fast, leaning forward.

I asked him to stop and breathe. I asked what he felt when Rashmi spoke. After a pause: "Like I'm a failure. Like she's listing why I'm not good enough."

We practised again. Rashmi repeated her point. Saurabh breathed. Then he said, slowly, "Some of that's true. I leave most of it to you. I'm sorry." Rashmi's eyes filled.

Only after that did he add his side about wanting to be included in decisions. Rashmi listened properly this time.

Homework: when a complaint comes, first name one true thing in it.

- Noor

qa.q: What did Saurabh say he booked for Diwali?
qa.a: Saurabh said he booked the cab for Diwali.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he answered so fast?
qa.a: Saurabh felt like a failure, as if Rashmi were listing why he wasn't good enough, so he got defensive.

qa.q: What did Noor teach Saurabh to do first when criticised?
qa.a: Noor taught him to breathe, name what was true in the complaint and apologise before giving his own side.

qa.q: How did Rashmi respond when Saurabh owned part of the complaint?
qa.a: Rashmi's eyes filled, showing she felt heard, and she then listened properly to his side.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a young husband who defends instantly against criticism because it feels like failure, learning to name what is true first.
